name: Skulpturenpark Waldfrieden
funding: The Cragg Foundation, set up by the Cragg family in 2005, runs the park Tony Cragg bought in 2006.
watch: Franz Krause built the villa between 1947 and 1950; it now holds the foundation's archive and offices. The park opened in 2008.
records_note: Names the Cragg Foundation as publisher in its legal notice.
affiliations_note: Run by the Cragg Foundation, a non-profit foundation the Cragg family set up in 2005. Listed in the Iconic Houses network.

overview: Sculpture park at Hirschstraße 12 in Wuppertal, on a wooded slope above the Elberfeld and Barmen districts (park's site, EGHN). German Wikipedia puts it at about 14 hectares in the Hesselnberg district of Barmen.

The sculptor Tony Cragg bought the abandoned Waldfrieden property in 2006. The Cragg Foundation, a non-profit founded in 2005, runs it. The park opened in September 2008 (park's site, German Wikipedia).
Named for the Villa Waldfrieden on the estate.

The lacquer manufacturer Kurt Herberts bought the estate in 1940, after a house of 1894 on it. Air raids destroyed that house in 1943. After the war Herberts commissioned the artist and architect Franz Krause to rebuild on the surviving basement, and the two-storey house and grounds were finished between 1947 and 1950 (park's villa page). The villa now holds the foundation's archive and offices.

On site: about 40 outdoor sculptures, three exhibition halls of different ages, a café, and concert series and education programmes. The second hall opened in September 2013 on about 5 hectares of forest added in 2012, and a round third hall in October 2017 (German Wikipedia).

Visiting: Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 18:00 from 14 March to 31 October and 11:00 to 17:00 from 1 November to 3 January. Closed 24 and 31 December and 4 January to 28 February 2027. Day ticket EUR 15, EUR 9 for full-time students and severely disabled visitors, EUR 10 each for groups of 10 or more, season ticket EUR 50 or EUR 40 reduced, free for ages 18 and under. The park says its hilly terrain gives only limited access for disabled visitors, and pets are not allowed (park's site).
details.funding_verdict: Skulpturenpark Waldfrieden: privately funded: the Cragg Foundation, set up by the Cragg family, plus ticket income and donations
funding: The EGHN page lists "Owner: Tony Cragg" and "Management: Cragg Foundation". The foundation's board is Tatjana Cragg (chair), Tony Cragg (deputy chair) and Michael Brämer (German Wikipedia). The park's legal notice names the Cragg Foundation as publisher and gives a VAT number, with no board or legal form.
Income the sources show: day tickets at EUR 15, season tickets from EUR 40, group tours at EUR 90 for 90 minutes, and a call for donations on the site.
details.bottom_line: Tickets, donations and the Cragg family's private foundation pay for the park. The weak points are that no funder list, accounts or visitor figures are published and that the sources do not say where the foundation's money comes from. Worth watching: whether the foundation ever publishes accounts or names sponsors.

name: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
funding: Federal government pays 71% of the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation's €275M operating budget, Berlin 14%, other Länder 7%. Sparkassen-Finanzgruppe is main sponsor, renewed in 2017.
watch: Governed by the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation (SPK). Colonial provenance is under restitution review.
records_note: Parent SPK posts annual reports 2016 to 2025 and budget figures; SMB names only supporter groups and patrons undated, and no council members.
affiliations_note: A body of the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz, sibling of the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin; runs about twenty museums including the Nationalgalerie sites, Pergamonmuseum and Museumsinsel houses. Member of ASEMUS, Deutscher Museumsbund.

overview: Group of Berlin museums, libraries and research institutes with collections of European and non-European art, archaeology and ethnology, spread over sites including Museum Island, the Kulturforum, Charlottenburg, Dahlem and the Humboldt Forum (Wikipedia, smb.museum).

Founded in 1823 by King Friedrich Wilhelm III of Prussia as the Königliche Museen, the Royal Museums (Wikipedia). It belongs to the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation (SPK), set up in 1957 to preserve the cultural property of the former state of Prussia (smb.museum).

Sites include the Altes Museum, Alte Nationalgalerie, Bode Museum, Neues Museum and Pergamon Museum on Museum Island, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1999. The Gemäldegalerie and Neue Nationalgalerie at the Kulturforum. And the Ethnological Museum and Museum of Asian Art in the Humboldt Forum (Wikipedia).

Visiting: admission is free for under-18s, people receiving benefits such as Bürgergeld, and holders of annual passes. Students, trainees in national service and severely disabled visitors pay half (smb.museum).
details.funding_verdict: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin: mainly public: the federal government, Berlin and the other German states through the SPK, plus Sparkassen-Finanzgruppe sponsorship
funding: The SPK's 2025 operating budget is about €275.3 million: federal allocations about €196.4 million, the State of Berlin about €38.6 million, the other Länder about €20 million. A further €143.1 million is construction money, about €138.7 million of it for new construction projects funded by the Federal Office for Building and Regional Planning (SPK budget page).

Sparkassen-Finanzgruppe, the savings-bank group, has been main sponsor since 2011. In 2014 it renewed for three years, covering exhibitions, cultural education for young people and external representation. In July 2017 it renewed for two more years, with the Sparkassen-Kulturfonds, Berliner Sparkasse and, for the first time, the insurer Feuersozietät Berlin Brandenburg (smb.museum press releases).

press.overall: Criticism is mostly of the SPK's structure and of restitution, not of the museums' funders. The strongest pieces are news reports of an expert review and of the Benin dispute.

items.title: Catherine Hickley, "Panel recommends dissolution of 'dysfunctional' Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation" (8 July 2020)
points: Reports, citing Die Zeit, that a panel of academic advisers commissioned in 2018 by Culture Minister Monika Grütters called the foundation "dysfunctional" and "structurally overwhelmed".
The panel proposed splitting it into four bodies: one for the Berlin state museums, the State Library, the Secret State Archive and the Ibero-American Institute.

items.title: Chiara Zampetti Egidi, "Overdue review shakes up Germany's largest cultural institution" (2023)
points: The board approved a reform in December 2022: a board of up to seven members, only two of them from the national museums, and greater authority and their own budgets for the institutions.
Quotes the Tagesspiegel calling the response to the reform paper "devastating"; financing decisions were postponed.

items.title: Catherine Hickley, "Yet again, a US court dismisses Nazi-era Guelph Treasure art lawsuit" (2023)
points: The descendants of the Frankfurt dealers who bought part of the Guelph Treasure in 1929 say the sale was coerced; their lawyer Nicholas O'Donnell argues that Germany's refusal to recognise it as coerced conflicts with the Washington Conference Principles. The foundation argues it is immune from US jurisdiction; on 13 July 2023 a US appeals court upheld the denial of a ruling on the merits.
Germany's Advisory Commission rejected the claim in 2014, finding the sale was not due to persecution.

items.title: "Row erupts in Germany over restitution of bronzes" (13 June 2023)
points: A news report, not an art-press essay. After Nigeria's outgoing president Muhammadu Buhari said returned bronzes would go to the Oba of Benin, German officials disputed the terms. SPK president Hermann Parzinger said the declaration did not put future returns in doubt.
The Nigerian art historian Peju Layiwola called the German reaction overblown and "an excuse" not to return the objects.
Berlin's Ethnological Museum holds around 530 Benin objects.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the museums is public money from the federal government, Berlin and the other states, plus a savings-bank group as main sponsor, and none of the reporting found shows a flagged funder. The weak points are governance and restitution: an expert panel called the SPK dysfunctional, and the Guelph Treasure and Benin returns remain disputed. Worth watching is how the SPK reform and its financing decisions play out.

name: blaxTARLINES KUMASI
funding: Art network and incubator tied to the KNUST painting and sculpture department in Kumasi.
watch: Ranked 69 in ArtReview's 2025 Power 100 and invited to the 2026 Venice Biennale main exhibition.
records_note: Wikipedia lists none and no source names a funder, report, accounts or board.
affiliations_note: Works from KNUST's Department of Painting and Sculpture; co-runs Kelas Bareng with Gudskul, Städelschule and Nordland, and co-organises the Wintanworks exchange with Art Hub Copenhagen.

overview: Artist collective, organisational network and art incubator based on the campus of Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi. It "works in association with, yet independent from, KNUST" (e-flux, Doreen Mende, 6 October 2026), and KNUST places it at the Department of Painting and Sculpture, Faculty of Art.

Formally instituted in 2015 to reform the KNUST College of Art's curriculum (The State of the Arts). Its ethos draws on kąrî'kạchä seid'ou's Emancipatory Art Teaching project, started at KNUST in 2003 (The State of the Arts), and e-flux names seid'ou as a cofounder.
Its name draws on Kwame Nkrumah and Marcus Garvey's idea of the Black Star (Brooklyn Rail, Jesse Weaver Shipley, 2026).

Members include Ibrahim Mahama and Bernard Akoi-Jackson (Brooklyn Rail). E-flux also names Tracy Naa Koshie Thompson, Adjoa Daiki Apodey Kisser, Kwaku Boafo Kissiedu and Kwasi Ohene-Ayeh as key figures.
Programme: four end-of-year exhibitions from 2015 to 2017 and "Spectacles. Speculations…" in 2018, with a network extending internationally (The State of the Arts).

Ranked No. 69 in ArtReview's 2025 Power 100, up from No. 81 the year before (KNUST). Selected for the main exhibition of the 2026 Venice Biennale, "In Minor Keys", where it presented "SLOW DOWN: CATTLE BATTLE AHEAD" at the Arsenale, with a video archive, a library, a Kente-weaving loom and a map (e-flux; Brooklyn Rail).
Visiting: its exhibitions are free (The State of the Arts).
details.funding_verdict: blaxTARLINES KUMASI: artist-run network working from the KNUST campus
funding: The collective is based at KNUST's Department of Painting and Sculpture (KNUST news release) and two of its cofounders, kąrî'kạchä seid'ou and Ediwn Bodjawah, live in the campus atelier houses (e-flux).
e-flux describes the group's economy as value passed on rather than accumulated, "transforming art from commodity to gift".
details.bottom_line: The documented backing for blaxTARLINES is its base on a university campus, from which an artist-run network runs free exhibitions and has built an international profile through ArtReview's Power 100 and the 2026 Venice Biennale.

name: Nuuk Art Museum (Nuuk Kunstmuseum)
watch: A 'generous donation from the Augustinusfonden' let the museum buy the Melting Barricades collection in 2024. Augustinus Fonden is a Scandinavian Tobacco Group holder.
why_flagged: A 'generous donation from the Augustinusfonden' let the museum buy the Melting Barricades collection in 2024. Augustinus Fonden is a Scandinavian Tobacco Group holder.
records_note: A municipal museum; its site links one annual report, for 2015, and names only staff, with no accounts or donors.

overview: Municipal art museum at Kissarneqqortuunnguaq 5 in Nuuk, described on its own site as Greenland's largest art museum (stated by the museum).

Founded by the businessman Svend Junge, who opened it as an art museum in 2005. After Junge's death the municipality took over the building, fixtures and collection in 2007 (museum website). Wikipedia states that Svend and Helene Junge donated it to the citizens of Kommuneqarfik Sermersooq.
Not named for a person.

Building: a church built in 1958 for an Adventist congregation, designed by Jens Johan Frederiksen, who was himself an Adventist. In the late 1990s the oil company NunaOil bought the church and its clinic and made them offices. A temporary exhibition room was added in 2007 (museum website).

Collection: works by European artists who depicted Greenland, such as Emanuel A. Petersen and Harald Moltke, and by Greenlandic artists such as Pia Arke (Wikipedia). In 2024 it bought the whole "Melting Barricades" work by Inuk Silis Høegh and Asmund Havsteen-Mikkelsen (museum website).
Visiting (winter hours, 28 September 2026 to 31 May 2027): closed Monday to Wednesday. Thursday 11:00 to 21:00 with free entry. Friday to Sunday 11:00 to 17:00. Admission 40 kr otherwise.
details.funding_verdict: Nuuk Art Museum: municipal, with a 2024 donation from Augustinus Fonden for one collection purchase
funding: Kommuneqarfik Sermersooq runs the museum; the museum's contact address is on the municipality's sermersooq.gl domain.

Augustinus Fonden: the museum says a "generous donation from the Augustinusfonden" let it acquire the entire "Melting Barricades" collection in 2024, and its exhibition page says the exhibition was supported by the foundation (stated by the museum). Kunstkritikk (2025) reports the work was shown at the museum until December 2024.

red_flags.heading: Tobacco money (Augustinus Fonden)
points: Augustinus Fonden owns Chr. Augustinus Fabrikker, which it uses as the holding company for its investments (Wikipedia).

Chr. Augustinus Fabrikker held more than 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group as of 1 May 2025; C.W. Obel held more than 10%, and the company's investor page lists no other holder above 5% (Scandinavian Tobacco Group).
The donation was made in 2024, so the funder is current.

details.bottom_line: The museum is run by Sermersooq municipality. Its 2024 purchase of the Melting Barricades collection was supported by a donation from Augustinus Fonden, whose holding company holds more than 25% of Scandinavian Tobacco Group.

sources.note: interview with the artists; not criticism of the museum
NPR report on the exhibition; does not mention funding

name: Museo para la Identidad Nacional (MIN)
funding: Small foundation museum run by the Fundación Hondureña para la Identidad Nacional. Donors not published.
watch: The board was named in Nov 2022 to steer the museum through 'the greatest financial crisis' in its history. The site's sponsor block is empty.
records_note: Nine unlabelled, undated logos show as pillar partners. The foundation board, appointed November 2022, is named in full.
affiliations_note: Run by the nonprofit Fundación Hondureña para la Identidad Nacional, which its site names as the body behind the museum.

overview: Anthropology and history museum in the former Palacio de los Ministerios in the historic centre of Tegucigalpa (Spanish Wikipedia, El Heraldo).
Founded on 19 January 2006, under the government of President Ricardo Maduro (El Heraldo, Melissa López, 24 January 2019). Spanish Wikipedia gives the same inauguration date.
It covers Honduran history from the pre-Hispanic era to the present (Spanish Wikipedia).

The building dates from 1880, built under President Marco Aurelio Soto, first served as the city's General Hospital, gained a second storey in 1933 (Spanish Wikipedia). El Heraldo's photo caption dates it to 1882.

Four thematic halls cover the country's geology, geography, historical formation and cultural diversity, plus a Copán Virtual hall and a hall of busts of national heroes (Spanish Wikipedia). About 930,000 people visited between 2006 and 2019 (Spanish Wikipedia). El Heraldo gave an annual average of 70,000 in 2019.

The Fundación Hondureña para la Identidad Nacional (FHIN) runs the museum. Its site describes a new phase tied to the museum's 20th anniversary, with work on renewing the museum, technology and education (stated by the foundation).
details.funding_verdict: Museo para la Identidad Nacional: private non-profit foundation
funding: The FHIN is a non-profit that runs the museum; its board was named on 25 November 2022 (stated by the museum).

Board: Thierry Jean Marie Ghislain de Pierrefeu Midence (president), Aline Flores Pavón (vice president), Arturo Zacapa (secretary), Ana Carolina Galeano Burgos (assistant secretary), Lorena Isabel Maduro Andreu (treasurer), Ruy Axel Merriam Rubiano (assistant treasurer), Leonel Zacarias Bendeck Nasser (fiscal), and members Lizzeth Guadalupe Villatoro Flores, José Alfredo Castillo Callejas, Hilda Mercedes Castañeda Moncada and Karla Sofía Simón Saide (stated by the museum).

press.overall: One piece, in Hyperallergic, criticises the museum's national story.

items.title: Annette Lin, "How a Museum Wields Its Power in Crafting a National Identity" (26 September 2019)
points: Argues that the museum presents Honduras as a Maya-centred nation although the Maya lived only in the western fringes of the country, and that nearly 20% of Hondurans identify as indigenous or minority.

Quotes the historian Darío A. Euraque, former director of the Honduran Institute of Anthropology and History, who calls this the "Mayanization" of Honduras, a policy dating to the 1940s dictatorship of General Tiburcio Carías Andino.

Says the displays do not reflect the Lenca, Miskito, Garífuna and Ch'orti' communities, and that the virtual reality and interactive displays paint a "sunny picture" next to the emigration of over 250,000 Hondurans in the last financial year, more than 120,000 dengue cases and nationwide protests during the author's visit.
Criticises the museum's national story, not its funding.

details.bottom_line: The museum is run by a private non-profit foundation, the FHIN, whose eleven-member board was named in November 2022. The press criticism concerns the national story the museum tells, not its money.

name: Ludwig Museum Budapest
funding: Hungarian state, with the Ludwig Foundation collection.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The museum posts narrative reports for 2005 to 2025 and budget accounts for 2011 to 2025, shows two undated logos.
finances_note: FY2025 income HUF 743.8M: about 66 percent state funding, 13 percent company and foreign donors, 21 percent own revenue (éves költségvetési beszámoló 2025, forms 01, 02, 04).
affiliations_note: The Ludwig Museum began inside the Hungarian National Gallery, holds Ludwig Foundation works on long-term deposit, sits in the Müpa building and commissions Hungary's Venice Biennale presence. Member of CIMAM.

overview: Museum of contemporary art in the Müpa Budapest building (formerly the Palace of the Arts), in the wing facing the Danube, with 3,300 square metres of exhibition space (Ludwig Museum).

Founded by the German collectors Peter and Irene Ludwig: the contract to establish it was signed in Budapest on 21 March 1989, and the Ludwig Foundation donated 70 artworks to the state of Hungary to establish the collection (Ludwig Museum).

The first permanent exhibition opened on 4 June 1991 in Building A of the Buda Castle Palace. From 1996 to 2005 the museum was housed in the A wing of the Hungarian National Gallery, and in 2005 it moved to the Müpa (Ludwig Museum).
Peter Ludwig, born in Koblenz in 1925, worked in the family chocolate company and began collecting in 1957. He died on 22 July 1996 (Ludwig Museum).

The collection has a Central-Eastern European character, with Hungarian art of the 1960s to 1980s shown through selected works. The museum organises an average of 8 to 10 temporary exhibitions a year (Ludwig Museum).
The museum has run the Hungarian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale since 2015 (Ludwig Museum).
The director is Júlia Fabényi (Ludwig Museum website; Emerging Europe, 2019).
details.funding_verdict: Ludwig Museum Budapest: public: a central government-funded body, with the Ludwig Foundation financing acquisitions
funding: Under a 2005 deed of foundation the museum is a central government-funded body under the Treasury, with financial independence; its supervisory body is the Ministry of the National Cultural Heritage (Ludwig Museum history page).
The museum states that its international acquisitions and professional programmes are still regularly financed by the Ludwig Foundation based in Aachen (Ludwig Museum).

red_flags.heading: Protest over the 2013 choice of director
points: On 9 May 2013 more than 30 artists occupied the museum. The group United for Contemporary Art demanded a new, transparent tender for the director's post; it said the Ludwig Foundation had endorsed Barnabás Bencsik, who was competing with Júlia Fabényi, whom it described as "Fidesz-backed" (ArtLeaks, 12 May 2013, press release of the artists' group).
The occupiers left the museum on 22 May and continued the protest in front of the Ministry of Human Resources (ArtLeaks).

red_flags.heading: The museum excluded a portrait of the prime minister
points: In May 2019 director Júlia Fabényi decided to exclude János Brückner's work "Here and Now", a mural of Viktor Orbán that visitors built piece by piece for the museum's 30th anniversary exhibition. Emerging Europe reports that she expected a negative public reaction and calls the decision self-censorship (Claudia Patricolo, 18 May 2019).
Emerging Europe cites no instruction from a ministry or government body; the museum itself acted.

press.overall: The two pieces concern the 2013 director appointment and the 2019 exclusion of one work.

items.title: United for Contemporary Art, "Enough is enough! (Ludwig Museum, Budapest, Hungary)" (12 May 2013)
points: Demands a new, transparent tender for the museum's director, and transparency in cultural governance, institutional and professional autonomy, and an end to withheld funding.
An artists' protest statement, partisan in its stance; the page names no individual author.

items.title: Claudia Patricolo, "Why did a Hungarian museum self-censor a portrait of Viktor Orbán?" (18 May 2019)
points: Reports that the director excluded Brückner's work from the anniversary exhibition and that the artist and Péter Bencze, founder of Everybody Needs Art, were called in to discuss it.
Quotes Brückner saying he refuses to "play the self-censorship game".
Not an art-press outlet.

details.bottom_line: The Ludwig Museum is a central government-funded body under the Treasury, with the Ludwig Foundation based in Aachen financing acquisitions and professional programmes. The documented issues are the 2013 artists' occupation over the director's appointment and the director's 2019 decision to exclude a portrait of Orbán.

name: Reykjavík Art Museum
funding: Municipal museum funded by the City of Reykjavík.
records_note: Posts its 2023 annual report; its parent City of Reykjavik posts consolidated annual accounts.
finances_note: FY2023 income ISK 704M: about 77 percent City of Reykjavik contribution, 23 percent own income, mostly tickets and shop (annual report 2023, p. 11).
affiliations_note: Reykjavík Art Museum runs three sites, Hafnarhús, Kjarvalsstaðir and Ásmundarsafn, and names Reykjavík Arts Festival, DesignMarch and Iceland Airwaves as festival partners.

overview: Municipal art museum (Listasafn Reykjavíkur) with three sites in central Reykjavík: Hafnarhús at Tryggvagata 17, Kjarvalsstaðir at Flókagata 24 and Ásmundarsafn at Sigtún 105 (museum website).

Founded in 1973 (Wikipedia). Kjarvalsstaðir opened in 1973 beside Klambratún garden, named for the painter Jóhannes S. Kjarval, and was the first building in Iceland designed for visual art exhibitions (Wikipedia).
Hafnarhús is a harbour warehouse built in the 1930s. Studio Grandi architects renovated it in 1998 to 2000 to house the museum (Visit Reykjavík). Wikipedia gives April 2000 for its reopening.
Ásmundarsafn opened in 1983 in Laugardalur, in the former home and studio of the sculptor Ásmundur Sveinsson, which he largely built himself between 1942 and 1950 (Wikipedia).

The collection holds more than 17,000 items, mostly by 20th and 21st century Icelandic artists, with holdings by Erró, Kjarval and Sveinsson. About fifteen exhibitions open each year and the museum also manages public art in the city (museum website).

The museum runs around 200 events a year, including tours for people with disabilities, and takes part in Iceland Airwaves, Reykjavík Museum Night, Reykjavík Arts Festival, DesignMarch and Reykjavík Cultural Night (museum website).
Hafnarhús is open 10:00 to 17:00 with late opening to 22:00 on Thursdays, Kjarvalsstaðir 10:00 to 17:00 and Ásmundarsafn 13:00 to 17:00 (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Reykjavík Art Museum: municipal: financed and managed by the City of Reykjavík
funding: Wikipedia states that the museum manages the city's art collection and that Reykjavík city is responsible for the museum's management and financing.
Its contact address is on the city's reykjavik.is domain (museum website).
not_related: the National Gallery of Iceland (Listasafn Íslands), whose website is listasafn.is. It is a different institution at Laufásvegur 12, with a collection owned by the Icelandic nation and its own sites (the main gallery, Safnahúsið and the Einar Jónsson Museum), not part of the Reykjavík city museum.
details.bottom_line: Reykjavík Art Museum is a municipal museum financed and managed by the City of Reykjavík (Wikipedia). Its collection of more than 17,000 items is shown across three sites, and the museum is responsible for public art in the city (museum website).

name: Jehangir Art Gallery
watch: In April 2013 the gallery and Mumbai police made Eleena Banik remove two goddess paintings. In 2006 it had a student cover a nude sculpture.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The gallery names its management committee with chairman Adi Jehangir.

overview: Exhibition gallery at 161 Kala Ghoda, South Mumbai, behind the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya museum (Wikipedia, gallery site).
Built on a gift from Sir Cowasji Jehangir, 2nd Baronet, in memory of his late son Jehangir. B. G. Kher, then Chief Minister of Bombay, inaugurated it on 21 January 1952 (gallery site).
Wikipedia says Cowasji Jehangir founded it at the urging of K. K. Hebbar and Homi J. Bhabha and paid the entire construction cost.
The gallery site credits the architect Durga Bajpai. Wikipedia's introduction credits G. M. Bhuta, tagged "citation needed", so the sources conflict.

The space has an auditorium hall, four exhibition galleries, the Hirji Jehangir Gallery and a terrace gallery for photography and visual art (gallery site). The complex housed the Samovar cafe, and the antique dealer Natesans is a tenant (Wikipedia).
Visiting: entry is free and hours of 11:00 to 19:00 are given by Incredible India and Outlook Traveller, not by the gallery's own page.
details.funding_verdict: Jehangir Art Gallery: run by a committee: the Jehangir family's founding gift, with no sponsors named
funding: Cowasji Jehangir's gift paid the construction cost; a Committee of Management runs the gallery (Wikipedia).

The committee chairman is Adi H. Jehangir and the secretary is K. G. Menon; members include Dilip De, Shirin K. Bharucha, Yogesh Kamdar, Vishvanath D. Sabale, Sushma Gaikwad, Narendra D. Vichare, Prof. Anil Naik and Nitin Gadre, I.A.S. (gallery site).

red_flags.heading: State censorship or punishment, two works removed, April 2013
points: Mumbai police and the gallery asked artist Eleena Banik to take two goddess paintings out of public view after complaints; Varsha Thakar of the Hindu Janajagruti Samiti was among the complainants (AFP via The National).

One painting showed Kali without her garland of skulls; the other showed a goddess-like woman with strawberries on her body, which Banik said protested the fatal gang rape of a student in New Delhi (AFP via The National).
Banik said she received threats, including a death threat, and was given police protection. Gallery director K. G. Menon confirmed the request but gave no details (AFP via The National).

red_flags.heading: State censorship or punishment, police visit and a covered sculpture, 2006 and 2007
points: In 2006 the gallery asked a student to cover the sensitive parts of his nude sculpture (Subir Ghosh, blog).

In December 2007 two policemen visited Jatin Das's show "Body & Line" and suggested a notice barring under-18s; Joint Police Commissioner K. L. Prasad said it was only a suggestion, and Das put up a "Not Under 18" sign (Subir Ghosh, blog).

press.overall: The censorship cases above were reported by a news agency and a personal blog.

details.bottom_line: The money is a family founding gift run through a committee, with no sponsor, flagged or otherwise, on record. The weak points are opacity (no reports, accounts or booking terms) and a record of removing or covering work in 2006 and 2013, with police involved in 2007 and 2013. Worth watching: who sits on the committee and how exhibition slots are allocated.

name: Victoria Memorial Hall
funding: The page read does not name the funder; it says more than 10 crores a year in allocated funds went unused, per a CAG report of August 2022 as reported by Live History India.
watch: A museum in Kolkata with the highest footfall of any museum in India. A CAG audit report of August 2022 found 53.7% of posts vacant, no soft copy of the accession register and storerooms without smoke detectors or sprinklers.
records_note: Ministry of Culture and Comptroller and Auditor General reports on it exist; none was opened.

overview: A museum in Kolkata that, per Live History India (30 Sep 2022), has the highest footfall of any museum in India, often over 2,000 visitors a day on weekdays, and the biggest ticket revenue.
The page read gives no founding date and does not say who funded the construction.

What is there: only 2.44% of its objects are ever displayed; the Rabindra Bharati Society loaned more than 5,000 paintings in 2011, of which the museum has exhibited 9; less than 20% of artefacts are tagged with RFID (Live History India, 30 Sep 2022).
Archive: the page read describes no archive or library.
details.funding_verdict: Victoria Memorial Hall: public museum; funder not named in the page read, with unspent funds flagged by the auditor
funding: Over 10 crores a year in allocated funds went unused, per the CAG report of August 2022 (Live History India, 30 Sep 2022).
The page read gives no grant amount, no named donor and no ticket revenue figure.

red_flags.heading: Governance
points: The CAG report released in August 2022 found vacancies rose from 30.1% to 53.7% over the previous decade, some posts vacant for 32 years, no soft copy of the accession register, no report on the physical verification of antiquities, storerooms without smoke detectors and sprinklers, insufficient metal detectors and baggage scanners, and several galleries closed for almost two years for renovation or repair (Live History India, 30 Sep 2022). The previous audit was in 2013.

Live History India reports that many posts are filled by contractual workers. Unverified: unnamed former insiders quoted by Live History India say unionisation is a factor in keeping permanent staff low.

details.bottom_line: The page read gives a public museum with a large ticket income and an audit that found unused funds, vacancies and weak records. Who pays and how much is not stated there.
details.website: https://victoriamemorial-cal.org (not opened; the site returned an access-denied error)

name: Biennale Jogja
funding: Organised by Yayasan Biennale Yogyakarta, a state-funded foundation created in 2010. The Yogyakarta regional government ran the 2019 edition.
watch: On 9 October 2026 it announced closure after 16 years, citing rising censorship and violence against activists.
records_note: Lists its patron board and executive but dated 2015.
affiliations_note: Uses the Jogja National Museum and Taman Budaya Yogyakarta as venues; both hosted the 2011 and 2019 editions. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

overview: Contemporary art biennial in and around Yogyakarta, Indonesia, run since 2010 by the Yayasan Biennale Yogyakarta (Yogyakarta Biennale Foundation).

Began in 1983 as the "Yogyakarta Painting Exhibition" at the Taman Budaya cultural centre. Renamed Biennale Painting Yogyakarta in 1988. Renamed Yogyakarta Art Biennale in 1997 and Biennale Jogja in 2003 (Contemporary And).
The foundation was founded in 2010 by Mella Jaarsma, Nindityo Adipurnomo and other artists (Contemporary And). The Biennial Foundation gives its launch as 23 August 2010.

Since 2011 the "Equator" series has paired each edition with countries around the equator, starting with India (2011), then Arab countries (2013) and Nigeria (2015). The first round ended with the 2021 edition (Oceania and Nusantara) and the 17th edition, "Titen" (2023), opened the second round (Biennial Foundation).
The 18th edition, "Kawruh", ran in Part I at Boro hamlet from 19 to 24 September and Part II across 11 venues from 5 October to 20 November (ArtReview, reviewed April 2026; the page gives no year).
On 9 October 2026 the foundation announced it will close after 16 years, saying it needs to "REST" (Biennial Foundation, ArtReview).
details.funding_verdict: Biennale Jogja: public: a state-funded foundation
funding: Yayasan Biennale Yogyakarta is described as "state-funded" and was set up to manage the biennale after funding crises (Contemporary And, 2015). The Biennial Foundation's profile says a 2019 news item described the 2019 edition as run by the Yogyakarta Regional Government and organised by the foundation.
A commercial gallery sponsored the 2003 edition, the 2001 edition was cancelled for lack of public funding, and funding was again at risk in 2009 (Contemporary And).

press.overall: Criticism exists of the curatorial concept and organisation of recent editions; none found of funding. The last two editions each drew a critical review.

items.title: Adeline Chia, "Biennale Jogja 18 Review: Occasional Moments of Brilliance" (2026)
points: Judges the concept of kawruh "not exactly radical", the edition "strangely ahistorical and apolitical", and questions the framework of "translocality and transhistoricity".
In opening week some videos were switched off and several venues were closed; public visitorship was limited and most visitors were international art professionals.
Warns the biennale risks becoming an "exoticised 'hardship' tour" for art travellers.
Does not mention funding.

items.title: Asep Topan, "TITEN: a new phase of Biennale Jogja" (2024)
points: The Equator concept accepts the centre-periphery framing it wants to challenge.
The 17th edition feels like scattered small exhibitions rather than a cohesive whole; accessibility problems and unclear information made some venues seem incoherent.
Does not discuss funding or the state.

items.title: Christina Schott, "A Biennale with Naughty Coded into its DNA" (2015)
points: Not criticism of the institution: traces the biennale's history from Suharto-era restrictions on critical art to funding crises in 2001 and 2009.
Links the near-collapse of the event to its "urgent need for ongoing, professional management".

details.bottom_line: The money behind the biennale is public and no flagged funder was found, but no budget, funder list or accounts were found for any edition. The weak points are the missing budget and funder information, and the closure of the foundation. The closure statement cites "increasing censorship, and violence against activists and protesters" and a regime that has "failed to recognize people's cultures", without naming an incident against the biennale itself.
